OP

>silly goyim, gold is for yids!

Very high margin overpriced Ben shapiro gold ad ?

Yes — the gold ads featuring Ben Shapiro (for Birch Gold Group) are part of a long-running pattern in which dealers often sell products at high premiums/markups over the actual metal value.

Ben Shapiro has endorsed Birch Gold Group since around 2016. It was one of the first (and remains the exclusive gold) sponsor of the Daily Wire. He regularly promotes them on his show (e.g., “text BEN to 989898”), interviews their specialists, and the company features him prominently.

• Standard bullion (American Gold Eagles, Maple Leafs, bars, etc.) typically carries a modest premium of roughly 3–8% over the spot (melt) price.

• Companies in this space frequently steer customers toward “proof,” “fixed mintage,” “commemorative,” “exclusive,” or specialty coins. These can carry 15–30%, 50–65%+, or in extreme reported cases even higher premiums.

A clear example from a 2026 Financial Times investigation: One investor put $350,000 into Birch Gold. The same day, the account showed a market value under $220,000. A key driver was 231 “Gold Liberty & Britannia fixed mintage” ¼-oz coins. Spot value was about $660 each; Birch charged $1,100 (roughly a 67% markup). She said she went to Birch because of people she trusted, including Ben Shapiro and Megyn Kelly. When she later tried to sell, the quoted price captured far less of the gold price rise than pure metal would have

Tucker Carlson has publicly said he was offered roughly $20 million a year to endorse a gold company after leaving Fox. The size of the offer made him question the margins; he concluded the money came from selling specialty coins at large markups (sometimes described as “twice” the metal value or more) to customers who often don’t fully understand the spread, then offering low buybacks near melt value. He started his own company (Battalion Metals) claiming lower, more transparent pricing.

I think it depends a whole lot on how you define free market capitalism, and it’s a little more slippery than people give it credit for. For example, the roots of free market capitalism can be found in decidedly global trade systems (slave trade to Saint Domingue/Barbados/ capital gained from imperial projects infused money into a lot of the proto industrial movement, and capitalism as we understand it wouldn’t exist without global connection. I’d argue that it has NOT existed without global trade systems underpinning it. It’s important I think to agree on what “capitalism” is first and foremost because a lot of people mistakenly believe that it is simply a society with a free market. For me and for a lot of historians/economists, a capitalist society (as opposed to a feudalist/socialist/communist/mercantilist one) is one in which the society is organized around accruing capital in order to reinvest and consequently secure even more capital. Reinvestment in the pursuit of capital is a constitutive element. One can see how you could have a small town with a lively market center that is not necessarily capitalist in that the pursuit of capital is not the organizing principle of the society. Romans were not capitalists. Egyptians were not capitalists. Both had thriving trade.

So far as capitalist is understood in this way, it’s hard for me to imagine how it persists without the exploitation of labor at the periphery of capitalism’s core. Historically, it’s nearly always happened this way (and I use the word “nearly” because there are perhaps some exceptions to the rule that maybe I don’t know about, but I can’t think of them).
